issues.legal_issue: A legitimate child of a Hindu parent and a non-Hindu parent who is brought up as a Hindu may be governed by Hindu law and be a member of the Hindu undivided family with the Hindu parent.
material_facts: The father was Hindu by birth and continued to profess Hinduism after marrying a Christian woman under a civil marriage law.
The child was born legitimately from that marriage.
There was no evidence that the child was not brought up as a Hindu, did not conform to Hindu practices, was not recognised as Hindu by the surrounding society, or converted to another faith.
The father expressly declared that he and his son formed a Hindu undivided family.
The property obtained by the father on partition could be ancestral property in relation to his son.
The dispute arose in tax assessments over whether the father and son could be assessed as a Hindu undivided family.
issues.conclusion: The child was a Hindu governed by Hindu law and could validly be a member of a Hindu undivided family with his father; the family could claim assessment in that status.
issues.legal_principle: The codifying Hindu statutes extended the meaning of Hindu beyond the orthodox concept. Under the explanations to section 2(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, and explanation (ii) to section 3(1) of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, a legitimate or illegitimate child is Hindu if one parent is Hindu by religion and the child is brought up as a Hindu. The Court also relied on the broad and inclusive character of Hinduism discussed in Shastri Yagnapurushdasji v. Muldas Bhundardas Vaishya, Bhagwan Koer v. J. C. Bose, Lingappa v. Esudasan, Mothey Anja Ratna Raja Kumar v. Koney Narayana Rao, and Ananthaya v. Vishnu. It approved the High Court’s reliance on Gowli Buddanna v. Commissioner of Income-tax concerning Hindu undivided family status.

rule.if: tax_status_assessment_dispute and legitimate_child and one_parent_hindu and child_brought_up_hindu and hindu_parent_continued_hindu and parent_declared_hindu_family and property_capable_of_joint_family_status

predicates.tax_status_assessment_dispute: A tax assessment dispute concerns whether a parent and child are assessable as a Hindu undivided family.
predicates.legitimate_child: The child was born legitimately to the parents.
predicates.one_parent_hindu: At least one parent professed Hinduism.
predicates.child_brought_up_hindu: The child was brought up as a Hindu.
predicates.hindu_parent_continued_hindu: The Hindu parent continued to profess Hinduism after the marriage.
predicates.parent_declared_hindu_family: The parent expressly treated the parent and child as forming a Hindu undivided family.
predicates.property_capable_of_joint_family_status: The property held by the parent could have joint family status in relation to the child.
predicates.child_can_be_member_of_hindu_undivided_f: The child may be a member of a Hindu undivided family with the parent.

issues.definition: When a tax status assessment dispute involves a legitimate child of a Hindu parent who continued to profess Hinduism, and the child was brought up as a Hindu, the parent declared a Hindu undivided family, and the property could have joint family status, the child can be a member of that family.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory rule governing succession after a marriage under a civil marriage law does not by itself prevent a Hindu parent and Hindu child from constituting a Hindu undivided family or the parent from treating property as joint family property.
material_facts: The father was Hindu and married a Christian woman under a civil marriage law.
The son was a Hindu brought up as such and was a legitimate child of the marriage.
The father claimed that he and his son constituted a Hindu undivided family for tax assessment purposes and treated the property as joint family property.
The Revenue argued that the rule directing succession to be governed by a general succession law prevented the son from becoming a member of the Hindu undivided family.
issues.conclusion: The succession provision did not impair or alter the joint family structure or prevent the father from treating his property as joint family property with his Hindu son.
issues.legal_principle: Section 21 of the Special Marriage Act, 1954 provides for succession to the property of a person whose marriage is solemnized under that Act, and to the property of the issue of that marriage, under the Indian Succession Act, 1925. The Court held that this gives the issue a collateral statutory right of succession on intestacy; it does not alter the joint family structure or the Hindu parent’s discretion to treat property as joint family property with Hindu sons.

predicates.tax_status_assessment_dispute: A tax assessment dispute concerns whether a parent and child are assessable as a Hindu undivided family.
predicates.marriage_under_civil_marriage_law: The parents married under a civil marriage law that provides a rule for succession to their property.
predicates.child_is_hindu: The child is Hindu and governed by Hindu law.
predicates.parent_treated_property_as_joint_family: The parent treated the property as joint family property with the child.
predicates.succession_rule_does_not_prevent_hindu_u: The succession rule does not prevent the parent and child from constituting a Hindu undivided family.

issues.definition: When a tax assessment dispute involves a marriage under a civil marriage law, a Hindu child, and a parent who treated property as joint family property, the succession rule does not prevent Hindu undivided family status.
